newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronaut's father defends Mir program.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronaut's father defends Mir program.

text.p: Colin Foale, whose son Michael is aboard the Russian space station Mir, on Thursday defended the Russian space programme from critics who question Mir's safety.
Foale also said he did not think his son should return to Earth before the normal end of his mission, nor did he think his son would want to.

"We have an enormous admiration for the Russian achievement with Mir," Foale told ABC's "Good Morning America." "And of course it is getting old and Michael was the first person to recognise that when he launched to it."
When asked if he thought his son should end the mission and return to Earth, Foale said: "No, I don't think I would, and I don't think he would either."

An unmanned cargo craft slammed into the Mir space station on Wednesday, causing loss of air pressure in one compartment, but the crew -- Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin and U.S. astronaut Foale -- were reported safe.
The collision follows a major fire in February and a string of mechanical problems affecting the life support systems.

U.S. Representative James Sensenbrenner, Republican of Wisconsin and chairman of the House of Representatives Science Committee, on Wednesday called for the U.S. space agency to begin immediately a comprehensive review of the safety of Mir.

He asked the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to comply voluntarily with legislation that would bar more U.S. astronauts from going on board Mir for a long-term stay until the safety tests are passed.
But Foale said: "This mishap has got nothing to do with age and I think we ought to retain our perspective of that."

Mir began repairs to its cooling system which was damaged in Wednesday's mishap, Itar-Tass news agency reported on Thursday. Tass also said Mir's crew turned the space station to face the sun to help boost power supplies.

Foale said he thought the crew should remain in space and finish its mission, adding "as long as they are safe and they can escape and as long as they can boost the power supply I think everybody concerned would want to stay where they are."
The British-born Foale is scheduled to return to Earth on an Atlantis shuttle mission in late September, but no firm date has been set yet, a NASA spokeswoman said.
